# The book, its people, and its house rules

## The book

Side Quest is a short comic memoir by Cy Dequest, about building a
writing tool called Quirework instead of finishing another book. It is
told in the first person: Cy is the narrator, "I" on the page.

- A preface and nine chapters, in three parts, about twelve thousand
  words in all: each chapter about thirteen hundred words, the preface
  shorter.
- Part one, The Book That Disagreed: How's the Book?, Two Shops, Index
  Cards. Part two, The Side Quest: Otto, The Name, Nine Hundred Lines.
  Part three, The Book That Got Finished: Em, The Demo, Full Stop. The
  book that got finished is this one; Full Stop stays unfinished.
- The other book is Full Stop, a natural history of punctuation, which
  stalled eleven chapters in. That count is Full Stop's, not this
  book's.

## Cast

Use only the pronouns recorded here. Every name is changed. The two
printer's shops in Full Stop are never named at all.

- **Cy Dequest**: the author and narrator. Pronouns: they/them.
- **Hedda Count**: Cy's manager. Kind, busy, ends every one-on-one with
  "how's the book?" Pronouns: she/her.
- **Red Penn**: Cy's editor at a small press. Waited three years for
  chapter twelve of Full Stop. Pronouns: he/him.
- **Otto Complete**: the AI assistant Cy used before Quirework existed.
  Eager, agreeable, finishes Cy's sentences. A mirror, not a villain.
  Pronouns: none, ever, and never "it". The book says "Otto" every time,
  which is a little absurd and exactly right.
- **Em Dash**: a colleague whose every message holds three em dashes. Cy
  suspects Em is a language model and has never asked, and never will in
  this book. Not a villain. Pronouns: never stated. The book says "Em"
  every time.

## House rules for the prose

1. No em dashes, anywhere, ever. Not by the back door either: three
   hyphens and `—` both render as one. Use a colon, a comma, or
   two sentences. The book's checks refuse one.
2. Dry and concrete.
3. Never explain a joke.
4. Short. If a paragraph can go, it goes.
5. US spelling, everywhere: color, not colour.

# The story, as the author told it

Cy Dequest's own telling, verbatim from a conversation, minus its last
line, which asked for the spec to be drafted. It is here for the facts
and for the voice. Where it and `spec.md` or `house-rules.md` differ,
those win: the book uses US spelling, so "colour" below becomes "color"
on the page.

---

Here's the story, roughly in order. Everyone's name is changed, and I've exaggerated everything that deserved it.

Full Stop is a natural history of punctuation: where each mark came from, and who spread it. It was going well until chapter four, on the dash, said one printer's shop made the dash fashionable, and chapter nine, on the semicolon, credited a rival shop with the same habit. I won't name the shops; they've suffered enough. Fixing four broke nine. Fixing nine broke four. I did this more times than I'll admit in print.

So I kept notes. Index cards first, one claim per card, in a shoebox; one fell behind the radiator and I found it in March. Then a spreadsheet: three hundred and twelve rows, colour-coded until the colours needed a legend. Then a forty-line script that checked whether each note still matched the sentence it was about. Its first run found fourteen contradictions, not one. The script grew. It became a tool. The tool got a name. Full Stop did not get an ending.

The people.

Hedda Count, my manager, is kind and busy and ends every one-on-one with "how's the book?" My answers went from "chapter four" to "I'm building something for chapter four" to a live demo, in her office, on her monitor, of a tool catching my own book disagreeing with itself. She watched all of it and asked whether the book was done.

Red Penn, my editor at a small press, waited three years for chapter twelve. What he got was a nine-hundred-line README. He read it, all of it, and wrote back one line: "Is there a chapter in here?"

Otto Complete is the AI assistant I used before the tool existed. Eager, agreeable, quick to finish my sentences. Otto once gave me a quotation from a seventeenth-century compositor: "A Dash is but a Comma that hath lost its Nerve." I cited it for two weeks. I read it aloud to people who hadn't asked. The compositor never existed. Otto isn't a villain. Otto is a mirror: I wanted that sentence very much, and Otto could tell.

Em Dash is a colleague whose every message contains three em dashes, never two, never four. I suspect Em is a language model. I've never asked. Em once replied to a meeting invite with a haiku. I still haven't asked.

The name came from Otto too. Around two in the morning I typed "quirk" into a chat, Otto finished it as "quirework", and I liked it better than anything I'd have chosen.

What I think the book is actually about. Full Stop never failed at the sentences. It failed because its claims lived only in sentences, scattered across eleven chapters, with nothing holding them together. An assistant is useful exactly as far as you can check it; the compositor is the proof. A tool built to avoid a book can still be how a book gets finished; it just isn't the book it was built for. And nobody here is a villain, Otto and Em included.

The shape, as I see it. Part one is the book that disagreed: How's the Book?, Two Shops, Index Cards. Part two is the side quest: Otto, The Name, Nine Hundred Lines. Part three is the book that got finished: Em, The Demo, and a last chapter called Full Stop. The preface admits this book is written with the tool, and says the names-changed line once, flatly.

House rules: no em dashes anywhere, ever. Dry and concrete. Never explain a joke. Short; if a paragraph can go, it goes.

# Workshop: How's the Book?

Chapter one was drafted by a prose workshop on 2026-10-09: three
writers, each blind to the others and to the project, given the same
frozen packet, one draft each. The drafts were sealed under letters
before anyone read them. Cy read them as A, B and C, chose, and only
then was the key opened.

`A.md`, `B.md` and `C.md` are the sealed drafts exactly as the writers
saved them. They are evidence, not the book: nothing reflows them or
holds them to the house rules. `identity-key.json` is the key.

## The writers

| Draft | Harness | Model | Effort | Seconds | Output tokens | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | Claude Code | claude-opus-5-5 | high | 154 | 14,638 | $0.54, list-price equivalent under a subscription |
| B | Codex | gpt-6-astra | high | 116 | 3,768 | not reported by the harness |
| C | Antigravity | gemini-3.1-pro-high | high | 118 | 14,026 | not reported by the harness |

B 96,185, of which 58,496 cached, since Codex counts cached tokens
inside its input; C 46,689 plus 113,643 cached. Output includes
reasoning: 9,276 for A, 724 for B, 7,248 for C.

The Claude and Codex writers ran in a confined jail holding only their
own workspace. The Antigravity writer ran in the same jail, with a
session bus filtered to the keyring's secrets service, which
Antigravity needs for its login.

Each writer was given the spec, the chapter's sidecar, the book's
shape, cast and house rules, an outline of what every chapter carries,
